title: Federal Judge Rules Pentagon's Blacklisting of Anthropic 'Illegal and Baseless'
excerpt: In a 59-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Rita Lin found the Trump administration violated Anthropic's First and Fifth Amendment rights by designating the AI company a supply chain risk
body:
• U.S. District Judge Rita Lin ruled the Pentagon's supply chain risk designation against Anthropic was unlawful retaliation that violated the First and Fifth Amendments
  • The 59-page ruling found the government wanted to make a "public example" of Anthropic for criticizing military AI use, not because of genuine security concerns
  • The case marks the first time a U.S. company was designated a supply chain risk under a statute previously used only against foreign adversaries

A federal judge has struck down the Pentagon's blacklisting of AI company Anthropic, calling the government's actions "illegal and baseless" in a sweeping 59-page ruling issued Thursday night that hands a decisive victory to the maker of the Claude chatbot.

U.S. District Judge Rita Lin found that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's decision to designate Anthropic a national security supply chain risk violated the company's constitutional rights and was "arbitrary and capricious" under federal administrative law.

"The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics."

— U.S. District Judge Rita Lin

How the Dispute Began

The conflict traces back to February 2026, when negotiations between Anthropic and the Pentagon over a defense contract broke down. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei refused to allow the military unrestricted use of the company's Claude AI models, citing concerns that the technology was not reliable enough for autonomous weapons systems and that domestic surveillance would violate Americans' rights.

https://x.com/DeepThoughtAR/status/2093277573417701653

In response, President Donald Trump and Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security. Hegseth then took the unprecedented step of designating Anthropic a supply chain risk — a label previously reserved for companies connected to foreign adversaries under an obscure government-procurement statute designed to protect military systems from sabotage.

The designation barred Anthropic from Pentagon contracts and required defense contractors to stop using Claude in military work, a move Anthropic executives said could cost the company billions of dollars in lost business and reputational harm.

The Ruling

In her ruling, Lin — an appointee of former President Joe Biden — found that the government's actions "constituted unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment" and that Anthropic "was denied the pre-deprivation process required under the Fifth Amendment."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Jtnp0kZUcXQ

Lin wrote that the evidence showed the government's actions "were based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its 'arrogance' in criticizing the government, not based on any articulable basis to believe that Anthropic would actually sabotage its model."

The ruling stated that neither the Constitution nor the federal statute the government invoked allows officials to "impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views."

A Clash Over AI on the Battlefield

The case sits at the center of a broader debate over how artificial intelligence should be deployed in military operations. The Pentagon has argued that private companies should not be able to constrain military action, while Anthropic and other AI safety advocates maintain that current AI models are not reliable enough for life-or-death decisions.

Thursday's ruling is the latest judicial rebuke of Hegseth's approach. Earlier this year, a separate federal judge in Washington, D.C. ruled that the defense secretary violated reporters' First Amendment rights with a restrictive press policy, and another judge found he infringed on a Democratic senator's free speech rights.

An Anthropic spokesperson welcomed the ruling: "We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology."

What Comes Next

The government is expected to appeal. A separate case filed by Anthropic in the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. remains pending, adding another layer of complexity. In April, a three-judge panel in that case declined to suspend the supply chain risk designation, creating conflicting legal signals that will ultimately need resolution.

For the AI industry, the ruling sets a significant precedent: companies that disagree with how the government wants to use their technology cannot be punished through national security designations designed for foreign threats.
